title: "How Does the Fed Set Rates, and Can We Predict Its Next Move?"
subtitle: "Modeling FOMC policy decisions from economic and market data"

```{r}
#| include: false
# Headline numbers come from the Prediction page, which writes them when it
# renders (_quarto.yml renders it before this page).
summary_file <- "results/rq3_summary.rds"
has_results  <- file.exists(summary_file)
if (has_results) {
  rq3 <- readRDS(summary_file)
  rk  <- rq3$ranking
  f1  <- function(model) rk$Macro_F1[rk$Model == model]
  best_ml <- rk[endsWith(rk$Model, "_Tuned"), ][1, ]
  fitted  <- rk[!startsWith(rk$Model, "Baseline_"), ]
  n_clear <- sum(fitted$Gap_low > 0)
  wc <- rq3$window_comparison
  wc_fitted <- wc[!startsWith(wc$Model, "Baseline_"), ]
}
```

Eight times a year the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) decides
whether to cut, hold or raise the federal funds rate. This project asks
two questions about those decisions: **how does the Fed set rates**, and
**can its next move be predicted** from information available before each
meeting?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!has_results) {
  cat("*Render `prediction.qmd` first to fill in the headline results.*\n")
} else {
  cat(sprintf(
'## Headline

- Across %d scheduled meetings from %s to %s, each predicted by models
  trained only on earlier meetings, the best model scores a macro-F1 of
  **%.2f**, against **%.2f** for simply repeating the last decision.
- A two-step **hazard model** with six inputs fixed in advance ("will they
  move?", then "which way?") scores **%.2f**, against %.2f for the best
  tuned machine-learning model, which sees all inputs.
- The gain comes from information about the Fed itself rather than the
  economy: its previous decision, where rates are (including the zero
  lower bound) and what markets expect. With lagged economic data alone,
  every model lost to "same as last meeting" ([What changed](changes.qmd)).
- Models that beat the best simple rule with a bootstrap interval clear
  of zero: **%s**. %s
- Old history helps: training on all meetings since 1986 beats a rolling
  15-year window clearly for %d of %d fitted models.
',
    rq3$n_test, format(rq3$test_from, "%B %Y"), format(rq3$test_to, "%B %Y"),
    rq3$best_model$Macro_F1, rq3$baseline_f1,
    f1("Hazard_Two_Step"), best_ml$Macro_F1,
    if (n_clear == 0) "none" else n_clear,
    if (n_clear == 0) "The test period is too short to show a reliable edge." else "",
    sum(wc_fitted$Diff_high < 0), nrow(wc_fitted)
  ))
}
```

## The chapters

| Chapter | Question | Methods | Author |
|---|---|---|---|
| [The data](data.qmd) | What goes in? | FRED and FOMC calendar, cleaning, publication delays | Course project |
| [The rule](rule.qmd) | How does the target relate to inflation, unemployment and financial conditions, and has that changed? | Regression, rolling coefficients, structural breaks | Course-project teammates (original) |
| [The regimes](regimes.qmd) | Do macro conditions fall into distinct regimes? | PCA and k-means | Course-project teammates (original) |
| [The prediction](prediction.qmd) | Using only pre-meeting information, how do model families compare at predicting cut, hold or hike? | Multinomial logit, elastic net, random forest, XGBoost, ordered probit, hazard model; expanding-window evaluation | Inuk Baik (extended) |

The rule and the regimes are kept as the team's original course-project
chapters, each with a short note on known limitations. The prediction
chapter is the headline and was extended for this portfolio;
[What changed](changes.qmd) lists every change and its effect.

## How it is built

- **One command rebuilds everything.** `R/acquire_data.R` fetches the
  data from FRED and the Federal Reserve; `quarto render` rebuilds every
  page. Package versions are pinned with renv.
- **No look-ahead.** Each meeting is predicted only from data published
  before it started, and models are trained only on earlier meetings
  (expanding windows, time-ordered tuning).
- **A fair comparison, not a race.** All models share one evaluation
  path, one score (macro-F1, where a never-predicted class counts as 0),
  and three baselines: always hold, same as last meeting, and a
  market signal from the 2-year Treasury yield.

Source code: [github.com/inukbaik/fomc-policy-modeling](https://github.com/inukbaik/fomc-policy-modeling).
